name: Prize crossword No 27,944
preamble: Seven solutions, not defined, are linked in this 50th anniversary puzzle

clue.text: Giving a lift from college with family in car heading towards London

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: C is a standard abbreviation for college
kin are one's relatives
a Jag is a Jaguar car
in Britain one goes up to London, whatever the direction

explanation.surface: Someone describes being driven back from college in the family car, bound for London.
explanation.walkthrough: A Jag is a Jaguar car. In Britain, travel to the capital is traditionally called going 'up' to London from anywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To jack something up is to raise it with a jack, so jacking up is lifting, as with a car on a jack.

clue.text: Boatman's led with a knave

indicators.note: what is led with comes first, so this piece is placed at the front

blocks.note: the knave is the jack in cards, abbreviated J
the setter refers to himself as 'one', so his is one's

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of leading off with a knave, as in a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is the setter, and a setter speaking of himself impersonally says 'one'. Terry Jones was one of the Monty Python team, a theme answer the preamble leaves undefined.
explanation.definitionFit: Terry Jones belonged to the Monty Python comedy troupe, which turned fifty that year, so the preamble covers him as a linked solution.

clue.text: Bitter, unending campaign meets habitual reaction

indicators.note: without an ending, the word loses its final letter
two things that meet are placed side by side, one after the other

blocks.note: a cause is a campaign one fights for
a tic is an involuntary habitual twitch

explanation.surface: A political campaign drags on so long that it provokes a weary, bitter reflex.
explanation.walkthrough: CAUSE loses its last letter to become CAUS, and TIC is attached.
explanation.definitionFit: Caustic remarks are sharply sarcastic and cutting, which is what bitter speech means here.

clue.text: In refrain: Nessun Dorma

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second
surface padding completing the aria's title

explanation.surface: Someone notes that Nessun Dorma has a refrain, as in a music quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: Neil Innes wrote songs for Monty Python and is often called the seventh Python, so he is one of the preamble's undefined theme answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Innes composed music for the Monty Python films and shows, linking him to the anniversary theme named in the preamble.

clue.text: Send off to get free hospitality? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: saying the opposite holds turns the whole sequence back to front

blocks.note: to mail a letter is to send it off
a lig is British slang for a freebie, such as a free party with drinks

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to dismiss a guest just to enjoy free entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send off' reads like a referee's red card but just means post. Terry Gilliam was the American animator among the Pythons.
explanation.definitionFit: Terry Gilliam made the animations for Monty Python's Flying Circus, so he is a theme member the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: Hanging on first article one included in funny script

indicators.note: something funny is odd or peculiar, so the letters come out in a strange order

blocks.note: A denotes first place, as in grade A
a is the indefinite article
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A comedy writer clings to an opening article placed in a funny script.
explanation.walkthrough: The three short pieces join the letters of SCRIPT and the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasite clings to and feeds off a host, so being parasitic is hanging on to someone for support.

clue.text: TV company takes in university youngsters

indicators.note: to take something in is to admit it inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: CBS is an American television network
U is the usual abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A broadcaster recruits young graduates from a university.
explanation.walkthrough: U goes inside CBS.
explanation.definitionFit: Cubs are young animals, and the word is also used of junior Scouts or trainee reporters, all youngsters.

clue.text: A person pursuing another of the same sex

indicators.note: to pursue is to come behind, so this piece follows the first

blocks.note: a chap is a man, a person
a chap is male, so another of that sex is a man

explanation.surface: A man chasing another man, a romantic pursuit between people of the same sex.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to Graham Chapman, the Python who was openly gay; the wordplay is a man following a chap.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Chapman played the lead in several Python films, so he is a member of the troupe the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: Specialised shops with a couple of bills for Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

blocks.note: a couple is two
a bird's bill is its beak
swap the first sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: Upmarket shops that come with a pair of hefty invoices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bills' suggests invoices from pricey shops, but here they are birds' bills.
explanation.definitionFit: A boutique is a small shop selling specialised or fashionable goods, so the plural names specialised shops.

clue.text: I had an accident with nail gun in the groin

indicators.note: an accident leaves things wrecked and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A DIY mishap: someone shot themselves in the groin with a nail gun.
explanation.walkthrough: The painful story is an anagram of I plus NAIL GUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Inguinal is the anatomical adjective for the groin region, as in an inguinal hernia.

clue.text: Learned about a dead (at first unhappy) parrot

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only each word's opening letter is kept

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for dead
opening letter of the word
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone researched a dead parrot, a nod to the famous Python sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: The dead parrot is Monty Python's best-known sketch. 'Learned about' looks like the definition, but 'about' supplies RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To read up is to study a subject in books, so having read up is having learned it.

clue.text: The way things are, not even a T-shirt fits

indicators.note: dropping the even-numbered letters leaves the odd ones, every other letter

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A resigned remark that, as things stand, not even a T-shirt fits any more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fits' looks part of the source, but the odd letters come from A T-SHIRT FITS read straight through, the hyphen ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a situation in its current state without change, exactly how matters stand now.

clue.text: 'No rest for the wicked', I moan, after besetting sin

indicators.note: to beset is to harass and trouble, and troubled letters fall out of order
coming after means placed behind, so one piece follows the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A guilty sinner lies awake groaning, unable to sleep for their besetting sin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Besetting sin' reads as one phrase, but 'besetting' jumbles both parts, and the quotation is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleeplessness means getting no sleep at all, a playful twist on the proverb about the wicked never resting.

clue.text: Show about America becoming American

indicators.note: one thing becoming another means it is swapped out for its replacement

blocks.note: circa means about, as with dates
A is an abbreviation for America
US is used for American, as in US troops

explanation.surface: A show about America that ends up becoming thoroughly American.
explanation.walkthrough: The final A of CIRCA is replaced by US. The answer completes Monty Python's Flying Circus.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus is a travelling entertainment with acrobats and clowns, a kind of show.

clue.text: Noted agreement in the US: review aid and tie in with end of quarrel

indicators.note: to review is to go over and rework, so the letters are rearranged
the end means the last part, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone signs off on a deal, reviewing aid and linking it to settling a dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the US' explains the single L: American spelling does not double it.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting your initials on a document signals approval of its terms, so the past tense means marked assent.

clue.text: Salvaged point and got even with current leader going ahead

indicators.note: the leader is at the front, so only the opening letter is kept
to go ahead is to be placed in front of the next piece

blocks.note: S, south, is a compass point
opening letter of the word
to avenge a wrong is to get even

explanation.surface: A sports report: a team rescued a point and levelled, with the current leader pushing ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The sporting surface hides a compass point and revenge, not a match result.
explanation.definitionFit: To scavenge is to gather usable items from waste, which is rescuing or salvaging them.

clue.text: Greek character goes by bike — you say this must be changed

indicators.note: what you say is heard rather than read, so the spelling follows the sound

blocks.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
a tandem is a bicycle for two

explanation.surface: A Greek man rides past on a bike, and someone remarks that this has to change.
explanation.walkthrough: The unstressed ending of tandem is pronounced like the Latin ending -dum.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutandum is Latin for a thing to be altered, singular of mutanda, as in mutatis mutandis.

clue.text: March sung by a politician in theatrical style

indicators.note: what is sung is heard rather than seen, so the result is a sound-alike

blocks.note: a hike is a long march
taken as written
an MP is a Member of Parliament
run together, the three pieces sound like the answer

explanation.surface: A politician sings a marching song with exaggerated theatrical flair.
explanation.walkthrough: HIKE + A + MP said quickly comes out as the answer's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: High camp is extravagant, knowingly exaggerated showiness, a theatrical manner of performance or design.

clue.text: Opposed by many people, the Spanish Inquisition's first rising

indicators.note: the first part of a word is its opening letter alone
in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so the order flips

blocks.note: a host is a great crowd
el is Spanish for 'the'
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Crowds resisted the Spanish Inquisition when it first rose, a nod to the Python sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: Nobody expects the Spanish Inquisition, one of the troupe's famous sketches; here it is EL plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: Being hostile means being antagonistic and set against something, which is what opposed means.

clue.text: Phoney hypnotists? No, it’s fatal to be embraced by them!

definitions.text: fatal to be embraced by them

indicators.note: saying no to something refuses it, so those letters are left out
something phoney is fake, so the letters are rearranged into a counterfeit

blocks.note: taken as written
these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A warning: phoney hypnotists are dangerous, and their embrace could kill you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No, it's' reads as a conversational reply but asks for I, T, S to be struck from HYPNOTISTS before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: These large snakes kill prey by constriction, squeezing it to death in their coils.

clue.text: Deli item left for hotel

indicators.note: one thing given for another is exchanged, so a letter is replaced

blocks.note: cheese is sold at a delicatessen
L is the abbreviation for left
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A note that a deli product was left for a hotel to collect.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting for John Cleese, who starred in the Python cheese shop sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cleese was a founding member of Monty Python, so the preamble covers him as a linked theme answer.

clue.text: Boatman's officer accepts a new start after drug discharge

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside
the start of a word is its beginning, so only the opening letter is kept
coming after means following behind the earlier piece

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
a mate is an officer on a ship, fitting the setter's name
taken as written
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The setter's ship's officer welcomes a fresh start after a drugs charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boatman's' is the setter's name used for a ship, whose officer is a mate. 'Start' takes only the first letter of 'new'.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to issue or flow out from a source, which is discharging.

clue.text: It looks like our security service's repressed and dissipated

indicators.note: a resemblance in print lets a figure stand in for a lookalike letter

blocks.note: MI5 is Britain's domestic security service, and MI5'S written down looks like MISS
pent up means held back or repressed

explanation.surface: A comment that the nation's spies seem buttoned-up yet secretly debauched.
explanation.walkthrough: MI5 is the UK's domestic intelligence agency; the 5 looks like an S.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissipated life is one wasted on indulgence, just as a misspent youth was frittered away.

clue.text: Ionised matter engineered as lamp

indicators.note: something engineered is built or rigged anew, so the letters are reconstructed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A physics note: charged gas has been rigged up to work as a light.
explanation.walkthrough: Plasma really is used in some lamps, which makes the surface read naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: Plasma is the state of matter in which gas atoms are stripped of electrons, an ionised gas.

clue.text: It's clear one is advanced

indicators.note: something advanced is moved forward, so it is taken out and reinserted earlier

blocks.note: plain means clear, obvious
a means one, as in a single item

explanation.surface: A claim that it is obvious someone is well along, perhaps in years.
explanation.walkthrough: In PLAIN the A moves forward one place, ahead of the L. Michael Palin was a Python, one of the preamble's undefined answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Palin was a founding member of the Monty Python team, so he is a linked theme answer under the preamble.

clue.text: Don Carlo, say?

definitions.note: by example: the answer is the first name of Monty Don, a British TV gardener

indicators.note: to say a name is to speak it, so the spelling may differ from the sound

blocks.note: Monte is the word that goes before Carlo in the name of the Monaco resort

explanation.surface: A question about Verdi's opera Don Carlo, as if offering an example.
explanation.walkthrough: The opera title is a decoy split in two: Monty Don presents British gardening programmes, and Monte Carlo is in Monaco.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer partners the surname Don for the well-known gardener, so 'Don' clues it by association with that presenter.

clue.text: Fellow making things up going on air

blocks.note: F is an abbreviation for fellow
lying is inventing untruths

explanation.surface: A broadcaster caught inventing stories while on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On air' suggests broadcasting, but the definition means travelling through the air.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling through the sky by plane or wings is moving on air, the literal sense of flight.

clue.text: Rothko finally using a mixture of it plain

definitions.text: Rothko finally using a mixture of it plain

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept
a mixture blends things together, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: closing letter of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: The painter Rothko, at the end of his career, working with a plain mixture.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: Mark Rothko made his colour-field canvases with this medium, often in plain blocks of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Rothko's large canvases of plain colour fields were largely made with pigments bound in drying oil, the medium described.

clue.text: One widely admired vocally

indicators.note: vocally means by voice, so the word is heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: an idol is someone widely admired

explanation.surface: A tribute to someone whose voice is widely admired, a famous singer perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Idle was a Python, one of the seven undefined theme answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Idle wrote and performed in Monty Python, so he is one of the linked solutions named by the preamble.

clue.text: Complaint from hollow, dozy guard about leader of escape

indicators.note: something hollow is emptied out, so only the outside letters remain
to go about is to surround, so one piece wraps around another
a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the word with its middle removed
a sentry is a soldier on guard
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A prisoner complains that a sleepy guard is the key to escaping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grumble but means an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors call an illness a complaint, and dysentery is an intestinal infection, so it is one such ailment.
